provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: The emitted program works directly in the visible coordinates. It treats palette[0] (originally black) as the background. It finds 8-connected same-colour components using reading-order flood fill, because shapes contain parts that touch only at corners. For each component it builds the membership mask inside the component's bounding box. It then counts the cells that disagree with that mask's mirror image. In the original orientation the mirror is left-right. Row reversal commutes with a left-right flip, and a quarter turn turns a left-right flip into an up-down flip. So the factory chooses the axis from d4 % 4 parity: column mirroring when the parity is even, row mirroring when it is odd. Rotation and reflection preserve the mismatch count, so the score has the same meaning under every transform. The component with the highest mismatch is the generator's single asymmetric shape, since every symmetric distractor scores 0. The program returns the grid crop of that component's bounding box, which is the same mechanism as the archived solver. There is no wrapper, no rotation of grids and no global colour unpermutation. The only specialised values are the background constant and the mirror axis.
draft_notes.limitations: Not executed by me. The constructor guarantees exactly one asymmetric shape and a gap of at least one cell between shape bounding boxes, so no ties arise and no crop can include part of another shape. If an out-of-domain scene had several shapes with equal maximal mismatch, the program would keep the first one in visible reading order. That tie-break is a fallback, not part of the puzzle rule. Shapes are assumed to be non-background colours, with background = palette[0]. Demonstrations are not needed and are ignored. I saw no fixture contradictions and no constructor defects affecting the visible rule.
